## What I would choose in your position

**Start by validating #1, with #2 as your strongest alternative.**

The first offers a useful combination of recoverable financial value, recurring work, and an administrative process you can learn without personally becoming a licensed technical professional. The second can support higher fees, but depends more heavily on hiring someone with substantial construction experience.

Your age matters primarily through **credibility, experience, and access to buyers**. Buyers will care whether you can handle their records accurately and produce results. A narrow service, a paid veteran reviewer, and a small documented pilot will do more for you than a large team or polished branding.

None of these is passive. Your initial job is sales, learning the workflow, quality control, and keeping cash collected. Outsourcing delivery does not outsource responsibility.

## How to use the $40,000

Keep most of it available until somebody pays you.

| Use | Budget ceiling |
|---|---:|
| Cash reserve and working capital | $20,000 |
| Paid industry specialist: workflow design, pilot delivery, review | $7,000 |
| Contracts, accounting setup, relevant legal advice, insurance | $5,000 |
| Secure software, basic website, email, CRM | $3,000 |
| Prospect research and targeted outreach | $3,000 |
| Contingency | $2,000 |

These are spending limits, not instructions to spend everything immediately. Keep personal living expenses separate; if the $40,000 must also support you, reduce business spending accordingly.

**Don’t hire 10 people with this budget.** Even at an illustrative fully loaded cost of $1,500 per person per month, ten people cost $15,000 monthly before sales, software, insurance, or specialist management.

## A practical first 90 days

1. **Interview 20 buyers in one niche.** Ask about transaction volume, unresolved dollars, existing staff, systems, and what they already pay to solve the problem. Seek evidence of the problem, not compliments about your idea.
2. **Hire one experienced specialist for a limited paid assignment.** Have them review whether the work is commercially worthwhile, build a sample deliverable using authorized or fictional data, and identify failure points.
3. **Sell two or three tightly scoped paid pilots.** Charge an upfront fee that covers delivery. Define the records you need, your deliverables, exclusions, and what counts as a valid result.
4. **Track actual economics.** Measure collected revenue, delivery hours, specialist review costs, errors, sales effort, and customer renewal interest. Don’t count disputed or hypothetical “savings” as success.
5. **Expand only after repeat purchases.** Add contractors as contracted work supports them. Build toward 10–30 people only when workload and collected cash justify that size.

For a straightforward administrative niche, an initial **50% delivery gross-margin target** is a useful screening hurdle: after paying delivery staff and direct delivery tools, roughly half the fee remains for sales, management, overhead, and owner earnings. Specialist-heavy work may need different economics.

**Plan for several years to build a business producing $500,000 annually for you.** Reaching that in year one from $40,000, without existing customers or industry expertise, would be an exceptional outcome.
